completion.text:
In May 1915, as the Lusitania sinks, a frightened American agent named Danvers entrusts an oilskin packet of vitally important papers to a young American girl, Jane Finn, believing a woman has a better chance of reaching the lifeboats. Four years later, in postwar London, two old friends meet by chance: Tommy Beresford, a demobilized officer, and Prudence "Tuppence" Cowley, an archdeacon's daughter who served as a hospital worker during the war. Both are broke and jobless, so they whimsically form "The Young Adventurers, Ltd.," offering themselves for hire. Almost immediately a shifty man named Whittington, who overheard them, approaches Tuppence with a lucrative offer to impersonate someone in a Paris pensionnat. When Tuppence absently gives her name as "Jane Finn," a name Tommy had overheard in the street, Whittington reacts with alarm, pays her fifty pounds as hush money, and then abruptly vanishes.

Their advertisement seeking information about Jane Finn draws two replies. The first comes from "Mr. Carter," a head of British Intelligence whom Tommy recognizes. He explains that the girl vanished with a secret draft treaty whose publication could now topple the government and spark a Bolshevist-backed general strike. Behind the plot stands a shadowy master criminal known only as "Mr. Brown," whose true identity no one knows. Carter hires the pair to find Jane. The second reply comes from Julius P. Hersheimmer, a brash American millionaire who claims to be Jane's cousin and who joins forces with them after a bogus "Inspector Brown" steals his only photograph of her.

Reasoning that a woman named Rita may have shadowed Danvers, the pair traces her to Mrs. Marguerite "Rita" Vandemeyer of South Audley Mansions. Tommy follows Whittington's associate Boris to a house in Soho, bluffs his way inside using the password "Mr. Brown," and overhears a conspirators' meeting led by the Russian Kramenin, where the general strike is fixed for the 29th. He is knocked unconscious and imprisoned, and he saves his life only by bluffing that he can locate the treaty. Meanwhile Tuppence, aided by the lift-boy Albert, takes a position as Mrs. Vandemeyer's parlourmaid. There she meets the famous K.C. Sir James Peel Edgerton, who quietly warns her off and later becomes their ally.

When Mrs. Vandemeyer discovers her and holds her at gunpoint, Tuppence turns the tables and bribes her with Julius's fortune to reveal Mr. Brown's identity. Before she can talk, she collapses at the sight of Sir James and Julius, and by morning she is dead of chloral poisoning despite the three of them keeping watch. Through her doctor they learn that Jane had been hidden at a Bournemouth nursing home, supposedly suffering from amnesia, but she has already been moved. Julius proposes to Tuppence, who realizes she loves Tommy and asks for time. Then a telegram signed "Tommy" lures her away. Tommy escapes the Soho house with the help of Annette, a captive French-seeming servant girl who cries out "Marguerite" as he flees, and he returns to find Tuppence gone.

The search for Tuppence in Yorkshire fails. Sir James then announces that Jane Finn has turned up in Manchester with her memory restored, and Tommy and Julius follow her directions to a cliffside hiding place, only to find a packet bearing the inked message "With the compliments of Mr. Brown." Clothes of Tuppence's are reported washed ashore, and the grieving Tommy angrily confesses his love for her to Julius. Afterward he finds Annette's photograph in Julius's desk and realizes that she is the real Jane Finn and the Manchester girl was a plant. Still unsure whether Julius or Sir James is Mr. Brown, Tommy plays them against each other and traces the girls to Astley Priors in Kent. A forged note signed "Twopence," a misspelling only Sir James could have made, tells him which man is the traitor.

Julius forces Kramenin at gunpoint to extract Tuppence and Jane, who reveals that she has feigned amnesia for five years to protect the treaty. Tommy then sends the girls to Sir James, knowing Jane will lead him to the papers hidden behind a Faust picture of Marguerite in the Soho prison room. Jane recovers the treaty, and Sir James reveals himself as Mr. Brown and draws a gun, but Tommy and Julius, hidden behind a curtain, seize him. He poisons himself with a capsule hidden in his signet ring. Without its leader the conspiracy collapses, the treaty is burned, and the general strike dissolves peacefully. At a celebratory supper at the Savoy, Carter reads from the dead man's diary of megalomania, Tommy is reconciled with his wealthy uncle, and Jane is toasted as a heroine. Julius and Jane become engaged, and in a taxi Tommy and Tuppence finally admit their love and agree to marry. The ending crowns the book's lighthearted theme that youthful pluck, loyalty, and plain common sense can outwit the most brilliant and ruthless villainy, and Tuppence sums up their future by declaring that marriage, like adventure, is "a sport."
